description: We are Lucas , a team of Computer Science students from Unicamp (Campinas, Brazil). We combine skills in software engineering, AI, and audio to turn complex Earth data into experiences people can feel. For Space Apps 2026, we’re taking on The Earth Information Jukebox: translating NASA’s Earth Information Center visualizations into real-time sonifications with spoken narration, so that anyone, including blind and low-vision audiences, can hear how our planet is changing.
summary: Earth Jukebox turns NASA’s Earth Information Center visualizations into music you can play like a record, so that blind and low-vision people, and anyone who closes their eyes, can hear our planet change. A 3D globe turns like vinyl, wearing a real NASA visualization as its skin, while a fixed chrome needle plays the strip of map passing under it, latitude by latitude. Every note comes from a value read from the NASA frame with NASA’s own colour bar, ruler or map key: nothing is invented, and no music is SI-generated. It is played live in the browser with real instruments and musical rules. Five records (sea surface temperature, lightning seen from the ISS, night lights, aerosols and sea level) are narrated in English, Portuguese and Spanish, with liner notes that explain every mapping and its limits. In a test at the hackathon, with music only and no narration, 5 of 5 listeners who could not see the screen, two of them people with visual impairments, heard the sea rising. Earth Jukebox combines technical and creative skills to make NASA data accessible to the people a wall of screens leaves out.
details:
The problem

NASA’s Earth Information Center tells the story of our changing planet on a wall of screens. About 43 million people in the world are blind (Vision Loss Expert Group, The Lancet Global Health, 2021), and many more have low vision. For them, that story is silent. The challenge asked us to translate sight into sound. We wanted a translation accurate enough to trust and beautiful enough to keep listening to.

What it does

Open the site, choose a language (English, Portuguese or Spanish) and put on headphones. The camera descends to the Earth, the needle drops and the music starts. The globe turns like a record wearing a NASA visualization. As NASA’s video moves forward in time, the music changes with it: you hear the northern oceans warm toward September, lightning follow the sun between the hemispheres, cities brighten year after year, and the sea climb centimetre by centimetre.

  • Change record swaps the visualization and its soundscape.
  • Drag the globe or the time ring to travel in time and hear what passes under the needle.
  • Mute or solo any voice, or pick another instrument for it.
  • What am I hearing? opens the liner notes of the record.

The five records

All five come from the challenge’s Resources tab and NASA’s Earth Information Center.

  • Sea surface temperature, March 2007 to March 2008 (NASA SVS 3912, ECCO2 model, MIT/JPL): warmer water gives a higher and brighter note. Northern waters play on strings, the tropics on piano and southern waters on glockenspiel.
  • Lightning, 2017 to 2023 (SVS 5011, Lightning Imaging Sensor on the ISS): a marimba hit for each latitude band with lightning. North is higher, and more lightning hits harder.
  • Night lights, 2012 to 2023 (SVS 5313, Black Marble, NASA/NOAA): more light gives more piano notes. Lights going out are falling strings, and new lights are rising bells.
  • Aerosols, 19 August 2025 (SVS 5669, GEOS-FP model, NASA GMAO): smoke on low strings, dust on marimba, sea salt on glockenspiel. You hear Saharan dust over the Atlantic, smoke over central Africa and sea salt in the Southern Ocean.
  • Sea level, 1993 to 2023 (SVS 5235, measured by the TOPEX/Poseidon, Jason-1, Jason-2, Jason-3 and Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich altimeters): one string note climbs a step for every centimetre of global mean sea level, up to 11.5 cm above 1993 at the peak in October 2023. A bell rings for each new centimetre.

How it works

  1. Reading NASA’s frames (open and reproducible). For each record, a Python pipeline reads NASA’s original files and turns pixels into values with NASA’s own legend:
    Dates come from NASA’s own files. For example, the date of every lightning frame comes from NASA’s labels.txt file, where we found and corrected a “2003” typo for 2023. The output is a grid of values for each 2-degree cell and time step, checked by automated tests. Anyone can re-run it or add a new NASA map.
    • the 0 to 32 degrees Celsius colour bar (the pipeline reads the bar’s own values back within 0.3 degrees);
    • the yellow lightning dots;
    • the light added above NASA’s own lights-off frame;
    • the colour key of each aerosol type;
    • the blue bar on the ruler printed in the sea level video (one pixel is about half a millimetre).
    • musical scales (mostly C major pentatonic);
    • at most three voices per record, two notes per voice and six in total;
    • arpeggios instead of clusters, because a direct pixel-to-sound translation is noise.
    • what you hear, in one sentence;
    • a data-to-sound table;
    • what to listen for;
    • NASA’s legend with a Hear the legend button, which plays the scale from minimum to maximum so you can calibrate your ear before listening;
    • the limits of the reading;
    • the NASA source.

Accessibility, the core of the challenge

  • Made to be used without seeing the screen: narration and captions in three languages. Press V to hear the date and current values read aloud with their units. When there is no value, it says why: land, no data, or outside the sensor’s view.
  • Full keyboard control (Space, arrow keys, V, R, L, Home, Esc) and visible focus. The scene is described for screen readers, narration goes to a live region, and a time slider gives the date.
  • Hear the legend on every record, including those without a numeric colour bar.
  • Respects reduced motion and reduced transparency settings. A 2D version opens when 3D is not available. No login and no install.

We tested it

At the hackathon, five people listened to the music alone, without narration and without seeing the screen: two people with visual impairments and three sighted volunteers with their eyes closed.

  • 5 of 5 heard that sea level rises.
  • 3 of 5 picked the warmer season of the northern oceans by pitch alone. This is a subtler difference of a few degrees on a single voice, and it shows us where to sharpen the mapping next.

We report every answer, including the misses.

Why it matters

Earth Jukebox opens NASA Earth science to people a visual exhibit leaves out, in three languages, in any browser, for free. It works as a sound layer for the Earth Information Center: the same NASA visualizations, heard instead of seen. Because the pipeline is open, any flat NASA map can become a new record. And sound reaches people in a way a chart does not: you don’t just see a line go up, you hear the sea rise, note by note.

Creative choices, and why

We took the jukebox literally: the Earth is the record and the needle reads it. It works like the radar sweep of NASA’s own Caldwell 73 sonification (one of the challenge resources), turned into a turntable. We chose clarity over richness, and real instruments, because beauty keeps people listening. But never at the cost of the data: the music can only play what the map says.

Honest limits

Each record states its limits in the liner notes:

  • Lightning, night lights and aerosols have no numeric scale, so they play relative strength, not concentrations.
  • The lightning sensor only sees up to about 55 degrees north and south, so beyond that is silence, not zero.
  • Aerosols over land read weaker than over the sea.
  • Sulfate is shown but not played, to keep three clear voices.
  • A very quiet vinyl crackle plays underneath. It is not data, and the liner notes say so.

Tools

  • Browser: JavaScript, React, Vite, three.js with React Three Fiber, drei and postprocessing, GSAP, Tone.js, zustand and the Web Audio API.
  • Data pipeline: Python, numpy, Pillow and ffmpeg.
  • Testing and hosting: Vitest (151 tests, plus pipeline tests) and GitHub Pages.
  • Instrument samples: VSCO 2 Community Edition (CC0).
  • SI: the narrator is an ElevenLabs SI voice, cloned with his consent from team member Lucas Souza, and the sound effects also come from ElevenLabs. Both are credited in the site and tagged in each file’s metadata. We wrote the code with SI coding assistants, under the team’s direction and review. No data, values or music are SI-generated.

Source code: https://github.com/eluaden/earth-jukebox

What’s next

  • Testing with Brazilian organizations for blind people (Fundação Dorina Nowill, Instituto Benjamin Constant, Laramara).
  • Exploring the globe by touch, with vibration on phones.
  • Adding more Earth Information Center records through the open pipeline.
  • Bringing the sound layer to the Earth Information Center itself.
